findings.description: AWS access key ID and secret access key are embedded in plaintext in the instance user_data script, which is visible via the EC2 metadata service and API to anyone with read access to the instance or Terraform state, allowing credential theft.
The security group allows inbound TCP port 22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing the management interface of the instance to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.

The security group allows all outbound traffic (protocol -1, all ports) to 0.0.0.0/0, which increases the impact of a compromised instance by permitting unrestricted data exfiltration or command-and-control communication.

The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true (nor a kms_key_id), so data at rest on the attached disk is stored unencrypted, risking data exposure if the underlying storage is compromised or the snapshot is shared.

The snapshot is taken from an unencrypted volume and does not enforce encryption itself, so the backup data inherits the lack of encryption at rest, increasing exposure risk if the snapshot is copied or shared.

The S3 bucket used to store VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (no aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration), leaving potentially sensitive network traffic metadata unencrypted at rest.

The bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource associated with it, so there is no explicit control preventing the bucket or its objects from being made public via ACL or bucket policy misconfiguration in the future.

map_public_ip_on_launch = true automatically assigns public IP addresses to any instance launched in this subnet, expanding the internet-facing attack surface, especially combined with the permissive security group used by portal_server.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true causes all instances launched in this subnet to automatically receive a public IP address, unnecessarily increasing exposure to the internet.
